This message comes from Schwab. At Schwab, you can get everything from self-directed investing to full-service wealth management, all in one place.
No matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how, you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
For NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman. Israeli soldiers have shot and killed two men that the military says attacked an Israeli army position in the occupied West Bank.
At least five people were injured in that attack. NPR's Ruth Sherlock reports this comes just days before Israel's elections.
The Israeli military told NPR that soldiers were positioned behind concrete barriers at a busy checkpoint close to the Palestinian city of Hebron when two attackers opened fire on them.
A firefight continued for about 20 minutes before Israeli soldiers killed the attackers.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered Israeli troops to prepare for a full closure of the occupied West Bank.
Closures like these have become more common, and Israel regularly imposes restrictions on Palestinian movement in the West Bank, with 925 checkpoints, roadblocks, earth mounds, and other barriers set up between and around Palestinian cities in the territory.
Ruth Sherlock, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
President Trump continues his campaign swing to support Republican candidates across the country.
Today, he's going to Fort Myers, Florida to stump. He's expected to rally in Georgia and Michigan this weekend.
Americans are turning out in huge numbers to vote early, according to the University of Florida's election lab.
Some 21 million voters have already cast ballots, according to political science professor Michael McDonald.
He tells NPR's Sage Miller that Democrats are voting at higher rates than Republicans.
Democrats aren't the only voting group voting early. It's up among unaffiliated voters.
And in states like North Carolina and Georgia, McDonald says voters of color are showing up in droves.
African-American turnout is up. Hispanics have more than doubled their performance at the same day in 2022.
Even though Republicans aren't voting at the same rate as Democrats, it doesn't mean that they're sitting this one out.
NPR's Sage Miller reporting.
Mortgage rates have dipped for the first time in more than two months, but NPR's Stephen Bisaha reports mortgage rates are still higher than they were a year ago and keeping would-be home buyers on the sidelines.
Mortgage rates fell this week to 7.32 percent, a small dip from last week.
This is for an average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage.
Kate Wood is Nerdwall's housing expert and says this does not necessarily mean rates have turned a corner.
Seeing, okay, this is the first decrease that we've had after weeks of increases, like, yes, it's exciting, but I'd say all the time mortgage rates do not follow the laws of gravity.
What goes up does not have to come down.
The fundamentals that have pushed mortgage rates up have not changed much.
Inflation is still high, and mortgage rates are still more than a full percentage point higher than they were a year ago.
Stephen Bisaha, NPR News.
On Wall Street, in pre-market trading, Dow futures are lower.
This is NPR.
NPR has learned that the Justice Department has opened a probe into Trump insider and Republican operative Corey Lewandowski.
This is according to a person familiar with the matter not authorized to speak publicly.
It is not clear what issue is being reviewed.
The inspector general for the Department of Homeland Security had been examining allegations of financial improprieties during Lewandowski's work at DHS.
Crows have small brains, but new research finds they make quick, accurate decisions, and Piers Pinghuang reports on the advantages of bird brains.
Kerry and Crows can take in visual information and make decisions about twice as fast as humans and primates.
Andreas Neder is a comparative neuroscientist at the University of Tübingen in Germany.
In a long time, birds have been considered to be dumb creatures, which is totally wrong.
Birds are really fascinating, and you see many instances that evolution really pushed them to the limit.
Neder and his colleagues gave Crows a common decision-making test, also used in humans and primates.
He said the fact that Crows did it faster shows an advantage to how bird brains are organized.
Since they're more densely packed than monkey and human brains, signals don't travel as far, so birds can process information more quickly.
The paper is published in the journal Science, Pinghuang, NPR News.
Forecasters say Typhoon Shampi is swinging by Taiwan with top-sustained winds of 120 miles per hour.
Earlier this week, those winds hit more than 180 miles per hour. This is NPR.
